en.title: Hospitality and Tourism: the whole course
en.short: What hospitality and tourism covers, how the degree is organised, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Hospitality is the business of looking after guests: accommodation, food and drink, and the service around them. Tourism is the movement of people away from home for leisure, business or other reasons, and the industries that serve them. The two overlap. A hotel serves the business traveller and the holidaymaker; an airline, a tour operator, a restaurant, a conference centre and a museum sit in the same value chain.

The subject is studied as a management discipline, not only a craft. You learn how a room, a meal, a trip or an event is produced, priced, sold, staffed, financed and made to last. It draws on economics, marketing, law, accounting, geography and psychology. Because the guest is present while the service is made, staff behaviour and quality matter as much as the physical product.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook and department regulations.

In Nigeria, universities award a BSc in Hospitality and Tourism Management or a similar title, commonly over four years, with the National Universities Commission (NUC) setting benchmarks. Polytechnics award the ND and HND under NBTE standards, and HND graduates may go on to a postgraduate diploma and then a master’s. In the United Kingdom, a BA or BSc usually takes three years, sometimes four with a placement year. In Kenya and Ghana, bachelor’s degrees commonly run four years, with technical and vocational routes alongside.

Master’s degrees usually take one to two years and end with a dissertation. Many programmes also require supervised industrial experience, called industrial training, attachment or internship, before you graduate.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics: what the industry is; the tourism system and tourist demand; rooms division, meaning front office and housekeeping; food and beverage operations; service quality and the guest experience; numeracy for the industry; tourism geography and destinations; events and business tourism; and the institutions and governance that shape the sector, such as UN Tourism (the United Nations agency, formerly the UNWTO) and national tourism boards.

Core topics: marketing; revenue and yield management; financial management; human resource management; law; food and beverage management; tour operations and the travel trade; events management; planning and policy; sustainable tourism; tourism economics; cultural and heritage tourism; information technology; entrepreneurship; research methods; ethics; and strategic management.

Master’s topics: advanced tourism theory; destination competitiveness and governance; analytics and forecasting; and research methods for the dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn the vocabulary first, then the numbers. Definitions matter: visitor, tourist and excursionist are not the same, and the exact cut-offs vary slightly between official sources, so quote the one your course uses.

Many topics are quantitative: occupancy percentage, average daily rate, revenue per available room (RevPAR), food cost percentage, yield. Work them with real figures and check the arithmetic.

For management topics, use a small case: a 60-room hotel in Kumasi, a safari operator in Nairobi, a festival in Lagos. Ask what decision the manager faces and what information would help. Read one current industry source regularly, such as a hotel group’s annual report or a national statistics release, and note the year, because the figures change.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Treating hospitality and tourism as one thing. Hospitality is the guest service business; tourism is the movement of people and the destination system.

Presenting one country’s licensing, tax or visa rules as if they were universal.

Quoting an industry statistic with no year and no source.

Dividing room revenue by occupied rooms and calling the result RevPAR. That gives average daily rate. RevPAR is room revenue divided by rooms available, or occupancy multiplied by average daily rate.

Confusing marketing with advertising.

Describing a tourism development without its environmental and community effects.

keyPoints: Hospitality is the guest service business; tourism is the movement of people and the destination system that serves them.
Curricula share a common core: operations, marketing, finance, people, law, planning, sustainability and research.
Degree length, award title and industrial training rules differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Industry figures change, so always give the year and the source.
RevPAR is room revenue divided by rooms available, not by rooms sold.
Use small cases and real numbers to turn definitions into decisions.

en.title: Introduction to Hospitality and Tourism
en.short: Definitions, sectors, historical growth, service traits, structure and careers.

sections.heading: Definitions and sectors
sections.text:
Hospitality is the provision of accommodation, food and drink, and welcome services for people away from home. Tourism is the activity of visitors who travel to and stay outside their usual environment for less than a year, for leisure, business or other purposes. A visitor may stay overnight or return the same day. The visitor economy covers all businesses and organisations that serve visitors.

Its main sectors are accommodation, food service, transport, attractions, events and the travel trade (tour operators, agents and booking platforms). For example, Amina travels from Kano to Abuja for a conference. She uses an airline, taxi, hotel, restaurant, venue and museum. Each is a separate sector, but together they form one visitor economy.

sections.heading: Growth and service traits
sections.text:
Travel is old: people moved for trade, pilgrimage, health and war. In Europe, the Grand Tour of the 17th and 18th centuries sent wealthy young men to study art and culture. In the 19th century, Thomas Cook organised group excursions in Britain, and railways and steamships made travel cheaper. After the Second World War, jet aircraft and package holidays brought mass tourism. The internet later changed booking.

These industries differ from manufacturing: their products are mostly services. Services are intangible, inseparable (produced and consumed at once), perishable (an unsold room night is lost), variable in quality and often require customer participation.

sections.heading: Structure and careers
sections.text:
Many hospitality and tourism firms are small, but large chains, franchises and public bodies also operate. The structure links private suppliers, government tourism boards and intermediaries such as agents.

Careers begin in front office, housekeeping, food service, guiding, reservations or events assistance. With experience, people move into supervision, management, marketing, revenue, human resources, planning or ownership. Entry is possible at many levels, but hours can be unsocial and pay varies by country and role. Check local qualifications and regulations.

keyPoints: Hospitality provides accommodation, food and welcome services away from home; tourism is visitor activity outside the usual environment for under a year.
The visitor economy includes accommodation, food service, transport, attractions, events and the travel trade.
Travel grew through pilgrimage, the Grand Tour, rail and steamships, jet aircraft and online booking.
Hospitality and tourism products are services: intangible, inseparable, perishable and variable.
Industry structure links private firms, public tourism bodies and intermediaries, with many small businesses.
Careers start in operational roles and can progress into management, planning or ownership.

en.title: The Tourism System and Tourist Demand
en.short: Leiper’s system, motivation and typologies, demand determinants, seasonality and basic flow measures.

sections.heading: Leiper’s system
sections.text: Neil Leiper’s model treats tourism as a system with three geographical elements: the generating region, the transit route and the destination region. The generating region is where tourists come from and where demand is created. The transit route is the journey and any stopovers. The destination region is where the main visit and its impacts occur. The tourist moves between these elements, and the tourism industry supplies services along the way.

sections.heading: Motivation and typologies
sections.text: Motivation is the reason a person travels. Push factors are internal drives such as rest, escape, novelty or status. Pull factors are destination attractions such as beaches, culture, events or easy access. They work together. Plog places tourists on a continuum from allocentric, who seek new experiences, through mid-centric, to psychocentric, who prefer familiar places. Cohen’s four types are the organised mass tourist, individual mass tourist, explorer and drifter. Both models simplify real behaviour.

sections.heading: Demand and seasonality
sections.text: Demand is the willingness and ability to buy tourism at a given price. Its determinants include income, price, exchange rates, distance and access, safety, available time, demographics, tastes and marketing. Seasonality is regular variation across the year, caused by climate, holidays, school terms and events. It creates peak and low seasons, affecting jobs, cash flow and prices.

sections.heading: Measuring flows
sections.text: Arrivals count visitor entries. Nights count nights spent in the destination. Receipts are visitor spending in the destination. Average stay = nights ÷ arrivals. Average spend per arrival = receipts ÷ arrivals. Example: a destination records 50,000 arrivals and 200,000 nights. Average stay = 200,000 ÷ 50,000 = 4 nights. If receipts are $30,000,000, spend per arrival = $30,000,000 ÷ 50,000 = $600. Spend per night = $30,000,000 ÷ 200,000 = $150.

keyPoints: Leiper’s system links the generating region, transit route, destination region, tourist and tourism industry.
Push factors are internal motives; pull factors are destination attractions.
Plog’s continuum runs from allocentric to psychocentric; Cohen’s types are organised mass, individual mass, explorer and drifter.
Demand depends on income, price, exchange rates, access, safety, time and tastes.
Seasonality is regular yearly variation that creates peak and low seasons.
Average stay = nights ÷ arrivals; spend per arrival = receipts ÷ arrivals; spend per night = receipts ÷ nights.

en.title: Accommodation Operations: The Rooms Division
en.short: Front office, reservations, housekeeping and maintenance, with the guest cycle, room rates and occupancy metrics.

sections.heading: The rooms division
sections.text:
The rooms division sells and cares for guest bedrooms. Front office handles arrivals, departures, keys, messages and guest requests. Reservations takes bookings and records dates, room type and rate.

Housekeeping cleans and prepares rooms and public areas. Maintenance, often a separate engineering team, repairs faults in plumbing, electricity, air conditioning and furniture. Front office and housekeeping share one room status system, so a room is not sold until housekeeping marks it ready.

sections.heading: Guest cycle
sections.text:
The guest cycle runs from enquiry to check-out and the tasks that follow. A guest enquires, then reservations checks availability and records a booking. At arrival, front office verifies identity, registers the guest and issues a key.

During the stay, front office and housekeeping respond to requests and record charges. At departure, the guest settles the bill and returns the key. After check-out, housekeeping cleans the room and front office updates the room status. Good records support repeat visits and correct billing.

sections.heading: Rooms, rates and metrics
sections.text:
Room types include single, double, twin, suite and accessible rooms. Rates may be rack (published), corporate, group, package or seasonal. They differ by country, city and hotel, so check the property’s tariff.

A hotel has 100 rooms. It sells 70 rooms at an average daily rate (ADR) of 40,000 naira. Occupancy = 70 ÷ 100 = 70%. ADR = room revenue ÷ rooms sold = 2,800,000 ÷ 70 = 40,000. RevPAR (revenue per available room) = room revenue ÷ available rooms = 2,800,000 ÷ 100 = 28,000.

Check: RevPAR = ADR × occupancy = 40,000 × 0.70 = 28,000.

sections.heading: Standards and teamwork
sections.text:
Housekeeping standards cover cleanliness, bed making, linen changes, bathroom hygiene and lost property. Safety rules include safe chemical storage, clear corridors, fire exits and reporting damaged fittings.

Rooms works with food and beverage on room service, minibar and function rooms, and with engineering, security and accounts on repairs, keys and billing.

keyPoints: Front office, reservations and housekeeping form the rooms division, with maintenance or engineering supporting them.
The guest cycle runs from enquiry and booking through arrival, stay and departure, then post check-out cleaning and room status updates.
Occupancy = rooms sold ÷ rooms available; ADR = room revenue ÷ rooms sold; RevPAR = room revenue ÷ rooms available or ADR × occupancy.
Room rates and room types vary by property and market, so use the hotel’s current tariff.
Housekeeping standards and safety protect guests, staff and property.
Rooms must coordinate with food and beverage, engineering, security and accounts.

en.title: Food and Beverage Operations
en.short: Kitchen and restaurant organisation, menus, service styles, purchasing, hygiene and cost lines.

sections.heading: Organisation and menus
sections.text:
Kitchen work is often divided into a brigade: head chef, section chefs and commis (junior chefs). The restaurant side has front-of-house roles such as manager, host, waiters and cashier. Clear roles keep service flowing.

A menu is both a selling tool and a production plan. Types include a la carte, where each dish is priced separately; table d’hote, a fixed-price set meal; and cycle menus, repeated over days. Structure moves from starters to mains to desserts. Menu engineering classifies dishes by popularity and contribution margin, helping managers promote stars and review poor sellers.

sections.heading: Service styles
sections.text: Table service brings food to seated guests, from silver to plate service. Counter service asks guests to order and collect at a counter. Buffet service displays food for self-service, often with carving or live-cooking stations. Room service delivers to guest rooms, usually with a tray charge and limited hours. Each style changes staffing, equipment and speed. A buffet may need fewer waiters but more display space and food holding equipment.

sections.heading: Purchasing and hygiene
sections.text:
Purchasing sets what to buy, from whom and at what price. Receiving checks quantity, quality and temperature against the order and delivery note. Storage separates dry, chilled and frozen goods, uses first-in first-out rotation and records temperatures.

Food hygiene prevents contamination. HACCP, Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point, identifies hazards, sets critical control points, monitors limits and records corrective action. Common controls are cooking temperatures, cold storage and handwashing.

sections.heading: Costs and example
sections.text:
Main cost lines are food cost, beverage cost, labour, overheads and sales-related costs. Food cost percentage = food cost ÷ food sales × 100. Prime cost = food cost + labour cost.

Example: food sales 500,000 naira, food cost 150,000, labour 120,000, overheads 80,000. Food cost percentage = 150,000 ÷ 500,000 × 100 = 30%. Labour percentage = 120,000 ÷ 500,000 × 100 = 24%. Prime cost = 270,000, or 54% of sales. Overheads are 16%. Check: 30 + 24 + 16 = 70%.

keyPoints: Kitchen brigade and front-of-house roles divide work but must coordinate through a service sequence.
Menu types include a la carte, table d’hote and cycle menus, and menu engineering uses popularity and contribution margin.
Table, counter, buffet and room service differ in staffing, equipment and speed.
Purchasing, receiving and storage control quality and cost, with first-in first-out rotation and temperature records.
HACCP identifies hazards, sets critical control points, monitors limits and records corrective action.
Food cost percentage = food cost ÷ food sales × 100; prime cost = food cost + labour cost.

en.title: Service Quality and the Guest Experience
en.short: Service characteristics, moments of truth, SERVQUAL gaps, recovery and cross-cultural guest contact.

sections.heading: Service characteristics
sections.text:
Services have four features that shape quality. Intangibility means a guest cannot test a stay before buying it, so staff behaviour, cleanliness and reputation carry the promise. Inseparability means production and consumption happen together: a meal is served and eaten at the same time, and mistakes are seen at once. Variability means service differs by staff member, shift and guest. Perishability means an unsold room or seat cannot be stored. Quality therefore depends on systems and training.

A case: Amina books a quiet room at a guesthouse in Nakuru, Kenya. The receptionist promises one, but a wedding is moved next door. The room is clean and fairly priced, yet the promise fails. Reliability matters.

sections.heading: Moments of truth
sections.text: The service encounter is every contact between a guest and the organisation: booking, check-in, a meal, a query, check-out. Each contact where the guest forms a judgement is a moment of truth. A guest may forget the room size but remember a rude reply or a helpful porter. Staff need clear standards and authority to solve small problems.

sections.heading: SERVQUAL and gaps
sections.text:
SERVQUAL measures service quality as the gap between what guests expect and what they perceive. It uses five dimensions: reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy and tangibles. Reliability means doing what was promised. Responsiveness means prompt help. Assurance means knowledge and courtesy that create trust. Empathy means caring, individual attention. Tangibles are physical evidence such as cleanliness and appearance.

The gaps model explains why quality fails. The customer gap is the difference between expectation and perception. Provider gaps include not knowing expectations, poor service design, failure to deliver, and promises that do not match delivery.

sections.heading: Recovery and culture
sections.text: Service recovery means fixing a failure and restoring trust. Staff should listen, apologise, act quickly, and offer compensation. In Amina’s case, move her to a quiet room and follow up. Cross-cultural skills: use clear English, avoid slang, ask how guests wish to be addressed, check understanding, and respect dietary and religious needs. Nonverbal signals vary.

keyPoints: Services are intangible, inseparable, variable and perishable, so quality must be designed into systems.
The service encounter is every guest contact; each moment of truth shapes the guest’s judgement.
SERVQUAL compares expectations with perceptions using reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy and tangibles.
The gaps model links the customer gap to provider gaps in knowledge, design, delivery and promises.
Service recovery should be quick, sincere, fair and recorded so the cause is fixed.
Cross-cultural guest contact needs clear language, respect for names and needs, and checked understanding.

en.title: Hospitality and Tourism Numeracy
en.short: Percentages, occupancy, ADR, RevPAR, yield, food cost, mark-up, currency and trip costing.

sections.heading: Percentages and change
sections.text: Percent means per hundred: 15% = 0.15. Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. A room rate rises from 40,000 to 46,000 naira: change = 6,000 ÷ 40,000 = 15%. Check: 40,000 × 1.15 = 46,000. To reverse a rise, divide by 1.15, not subtract 15%: 46,000 ÷ 1.15 = 40,000.

sections.heading: Rooms arithmetic
sections.text:
Occupancy percentage = rooms sold ÷ rooms available × 100. Average daily rate (ADR) = room revenue ÷ rooms sold. Revenue per available room (RevPAR) = room revenue ÷ rooms available = ADR × occupancy. Yield = actual room revenue ÷ (rooms available × rack rate) × 100, where rack rate is the hotel’s published full price.

A 100-room hotel sells 72 rooms, earning 2,160,000 naira. Occupancy = 72 ÷ 100 = 72%. ADR = 2,160,000 ÷ 72 = 30,000. RevPAR = 2,160,000 ÷ 100 = 21,600; check 30,000 × 0.72 = 21,600. At a 40,000 rack rate, yield = 2,160,000 ÷ 4,000,000 = 54%.

sections.heading: Food cost and margin
sections.text:
Food cost percentage = cost of food sold ÷ food sales × 100. Food costing 12,000 naira sold for 30,000 gives 40%.

Mark-up is profit as a percentage of cost; margin is profit as a percentage of selling price. Cost 100, price 150: mark-up = 50 ÷ 100 = 50%; margin = 50 ÷ 150 = 33.3%. Price = cost × (1 + mark-up) = cost ÷ (1 − margin). Check: 100 ÷ (1 − 0.3333) = 150.

sections.heading: Currency, time and trips
sections.text:
Convert currency by multiplying by the exchange rate: 500 US dollars at 1,500 naira per dollar = 750,000 naira; check by dividing back.

Time zones are offsets from UTC, some by half hours. Lagos is UTC+1; London is UTC+0 in winter. A flight leaving Lagos at 09:00 taking 6 hours lands at 14:00 UTC: 14:00 in London, 15:00 in Lagos.

Trip cost = transport + (nights × room rate) + meals + fees + contingency (money set aside for unexpected costs). Add the items, then add contingency as a percentage of the subtotal.

keyPoints: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
Occupancy = rooms sold ÷ rooms available × 100; ADR = room revenue ÷ rooms sold.
RevPAR = room revenue ÷ rooms available = ADR × occupancy.
Food cost percentage = cost of food sold ÷ food sales × 100.
Mark-up is based on cost and margin on selling price; price = cost × (1 + mark-up) = cost ÷ (1 − margin).
Convert currency by multiplying by the rate and check by dividing back; exchange rates change, so use the current rate. Trip cost adds transport, nights × rate, meals, fees and contingency.

en.title: Tourism Geography and Destinations
en.short: Destination types, climate and access, world regions, and African and Nigerian attractions.

sections.heading: Destinations and attractions
sections.text: A destination is a place visitors choose to travel to and stay in. An attraction is a feature that draws them. Natural attractions come from the environment: parks, waterfalls, beaches and mountains. Cultural attractions express ways of life: festivals, museums, religious sites and heritage buildings. Built attractions are made for visitors, such as theme parks, resorts and conference centres. Many destinations mix all three. Nigeria’s Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove is natural and cultural.

sections.heading: Climate, season and access
sections.text: Climate affects comfort and timing. Season is the period when demand rises or falls because of weather, holidays or festivals. Accessibility means how easy a place is to reach and move around: transport, roads, visas, cost and safety. Poor access can keep visitors away. For example, a student in Lagos planning a trip to Yankari National Park may prefer the dry season, when roads are easier and wildlife is easier to see. The rainy season brings greener scenery but can make roads difficult.

sections.heading: World tourism regions
sections.text: UN Tourism (the UN agency) groups countries into five regions: Africa, the Americas, Asia and the Pacific, Europe, and the Middle East. Europe has cultural cities and coastal resorts. Asia and the Pacific has islands and cities. The Americas range from North American cities to Caribbean beaches. The Middle East offers desert, religious and city tourism. Africa is known for wildlife, landscapes and heritage. These regions organise data, not quality.

sections.heading: Africa and Nigeria
sections.text: Africa has many destinations. Victoria Falls, on the Zambia-Zimbabwe border, is natural. The Serengeti in Tanzania is famous for wildlife. The Pyramids of Giza in Egypt are cultural heritage. Table Mountain in South Africa is natural, and Marrakech in Morocco is a cultural city. In Nigeria, Yankari National Park and Wikki Warm Springs are natural. Obudu Mountain Resort offers mountain scenery. Olumo Rock is cultural and natural. Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove and Sukur Cultural Landscape are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Check current transport.

keyPoints: An attraction draws visitors; a destination is the place they travel to and stay in.
Attractions are natural, cultural or built, and many destinations combine the three.
Climate, season and accessibility can shape destination choice as much as the attraction itself.
UN Tourism groups countries into Africa, the Americas, Asia and the Pacific, Europe, and the Middle East.
Africa offers wildlife, heritage and coastal destinations, and Nigeria has natural and cultural sites such as Yankari National Park and Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove.
Transport, safety and opening conditions change, so check current official information before travelling.

en.title: Events and Business Tourism: Scope and Planning
en.short: Festivals, conferences, exhibitions, sports and weddings, MICE travel and the event planning cycle.

sections.heading: Event scope
sections.text: An event is a planned gathering of people for a purpose. The scope is wide: festivals and cultural celebrations, conferences and meetings, exhibitions and trade fairs, sports events, and weddings or private celebrations. Business events are often grouped as MICE: Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions. Incentive travel is a reward trip offered by an employer. Business tourism is travel for work-related purposes. Business travel, its main form, means travel for work, including meetings and conferences, and it may include some leisure time. MICE is a major part of business tourism, but definitions vary by country and organisation.

sections.heading: Planning cycle
sections.text: The basic event planning cycle has stages. First, the concept and aims state why the event exists and who it serves. Second, feasibility checks the market, venue, budget, risks and permissions. Third, detailed planning covers the programme, suppliers, staffing, marketing, ticketing and safety. Fourth, delivery runs the event on the day. Fifth, evaluation reviews attendance, spending, feedback and problems. Good planners loop back: lessons from evaluation shape the next event.

sections.heading: Why events matter
sections.text: Events can bring economic and social benefits. Visitors spend on accommodation, food, transport, venues and local goods, which supports jobs and tax revenue. Events can improve infrastructure and raise a destination’s profile. Socially, they can celebrate culture, build community pride and create shared experiences. Costs also exist: crowding, higher prices, waste, noise and pressure on local services. Planners should weigh benefits against these costs and consult residents.

sections.heading: Destination links
sections.text: Events, destinations and hospitality providers are linked. A destination’s image, access and venues help attract events; events in turn attract visitors who need hotels, restaurants, transport and attractions. Hospitality firms can package rooms, meals and services for delegates. A made-up case: a hotel in Kigali hosts a three-day conference for 200 delegates. The hotel earns room and meal revenue, while taxi drivers, cafes and craft sellers gain spending. Organisers must still plan rooms, catering, safety and evaluation.

keyPoints: Events are planned gatherings; their scope includes festivals, conferences, exhibitions, sports events and weddings.
MICE stands for Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions.
Business tourism is travel for work-related purposes, including meetings and conferences.
The planning cycle runs from concept and feasibility through detailed planning and delivery to evaluation.
Events bring visitor spending, jobs and destination promotion, but also crowding and other costs.
Events link destinations with hotels, food service, transport and venues.

en.title: Tourism Institutions and Governance
en.short: Covers global tourism bodies, national policy and law, industry associations, and accommodation grading.

sections.heading: Global bodies
sections.text:
UN Tourism, formerly the UN World Tourism Organization (UNWTO), is the United Nations agency for tourism. It collects statistics, advises governments, promotes sustainable tourism and publishes guidance. It does not own hotels or airlines.

 The World Travel and Tourism Council (WTTC) is a private-sector membership body. It researches travel and tourism’s economic impact and lobbies governments. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) is an airline trade association. It sets commercial standards, runs the IATA Operational Safety Audit (IOSA) and the Billing and Settlement Plan (BSP). It is not a tourism ministry.

sections.heading: National policy and law
sections.text:
National ministries set tourism policy. Government decides on visas, taxes, infrastructure and licensing. National tourism boards usually market the country and may develop products, license businesses or grade accommodation. Tourism legislation sets rules for registration, safety, consumer protection and planning.

 In Nigeria, the federal ministry responsible for tourism sets policy, and the Nigerian Tourism Development Corporation (NTDC) has development and regulatory functions; state governments also act. In South Africa, the Department of Tourism sets policy and South African Tourism markets the country. Check current national sources because ministries and laws change.

sections.heading: Associations and grading
sections.text:
Industry associations are member bodies for hotels, tour operators, travel agents or airlines. They lobby, share information, train staff and set voluntary codes. They do not replace government law.

 Accommodation grading is a rating scheme, often using stars, run by a national board or private body. It assesses facilities, cleanliness, safety and service. Schemes differ by country and change, so check the current official criteria. South Africa’s Tourism Grading Council of South Africa awards stars. Suppose Amina opens a guest house in Abuja. She registers under Nigerian rules, joins a hotel association and applies for grading. The grade helps marketing, but it is not a global passport.

keyPoints: UN Tourism is the UN agency for tourism policy, statistics and advice.
WTTC is a private-sector council for research and advocacy.
IATA is an airline trade body for standards, safety audit and settlement.
National ministries set policy; legislation sets the rules; boards market and may license or grade.
Industry associations support members and set voluntary codes but do not replace law.
Accommodation grading is country-specific; check current official criteria.

en.title: Hospitality and tourism marketing
en.short: The 7Ps, segmentation and positioning, branding, distribution, pricing and digital marketing.

sections.heading: The extended mix
sections.text:
The marketing mix is the set of controllable tools a firm uses to win customers. For services, the traditional four Ps (product, price, place, promotion) are extended to seven. People covers staff and their service attitude. Process covers how the service is delivered, from booking to check-out. Physical evidence covers tangible cues such as cleanliness, signage and uniforms. These matter because hospitality and tourism services are intangible, produced and consumed together, variable and perishable (an unsold room night is lost forever).

A safari lodge’s product is the room, meals and game drive. Its price may be per night. Place is the lodge and the booking channels. Promotion is advertising and public relations. Staff, check-in process and the look of the room complete the mix.

sections.heading: Segmentation and positioning
sections.text:
Segmentation divides a market into groups with similar needs, for example by trip purpose, income or behaviour. Targeting chooses which groups to serve. Positioning is the place a brand holds in the customer’s mind. A Lagos business hotel might target corporate travellers and position itself on reliable Wi-Fi and meeting rooms.

Branding makes a promise and keeps it. Loyalty programmes reward repeat guests, while customer relationship management (CRM) systems help the firm track and serve them. Loyalty comes from consistent service, not points alone.

sections.heading: Distribution and pricing
sections.text:
Distribution is how customers find and buy. Travel agents sell to the public. Tour operators combine transport, accommodation and activities into packages. Global distribution systems (GDS), such as Amadeus, Sabre and Travelport, let agents book flights and rooms. Online travel agencies (OTAs), such as Booking.com and Expedia, sell online and charge commission.

Pricing approaches include cost-plus, competition-based and demand-based. Perishability encourages dynamic pricing, where rates are adjusted as demand changes. A room sold at $120 through an OTA charging 15% commission leaves 120 − 18 = $102. A direct booking costing $8 in marketing leaves $112.

sections.heading: Digital and social media
sections.text: Digital marketing uses search, email, websites and social media. Reviews and user-generated content shape trust. Firms should answer reviews and make direct booking easy. Paid social media and influencers can reach specific segments, but results must be measured.

keyPoints: The 7Ps add people, process and physical evidence to the four Ps.
Segmentation divides, targeting selects, positioning shapes the brand’s place in the mind.
Branding is a promise kept through consistent service; loyalty schemes support but cannot replace it.
Travel agents, tour operators, GDS and OTAs are distribution intermediaries; each has a cost.
Net revenue from an OTA booking = rate × (1 − commission rate).
Digital and social media marketing must be measured and linked to direct bookings.

en.title: Revenue and Yield Management
en.short: Covers capacity, forecasting, rate fencing, RevPAR, overbooking, channels and revenue systems.

sections.heading: Capacity and forecasting
sections.text: Hotel rooms are capacity. In the short run the number of rooms is fixed, and an unsold room night cannot be stored and sold later. This is perishability. Demand forecasting estimates future occupancy by date, segment and rate. It uses past bookings, booking pace (how bookings build over time), seasonality, local events and market data. A forecast is a range, not a certainty, so revenue managers update it as the arrival date approaches.

sections.heading: Pricing and RevPAR
sections.text:
Rate fencing means using conditions to separate price-sensitive guests from those willing to pay more. Fences include advance purchase, non-refundable terms, minimum stay and membership rates. Yield management allocates limited rooms among segments and rates to maximise contribution, not occupancy alone. RevPAR (revenue per available room) = room revenue ÷ available rooms, or ADR × occupancy. ADR is average daily rate.

Example: 100-room hotel has 30 days, so 3,000 available room nights. It sells 2,400 room nights for room revenue of 180,000. Occupancy = 2,400 ÷ 3,000 = 80%. ADR = 180,000 ÷ 2,400 = 75. RevPAR = 180,000 ÷ 3,000 = 60. Check: 75 × 0.80 = 60. A discount that fills rooms but lowers RevPAR may reduce profit.

sections.heading: Overbooking and channels
sections.text: Overbooking accepts more reservations than rooms because some guests do not arrive (no-shows) or cancel late. Expected no-shows = bookings × no-show rate. A policy must state walk procedures (moving guests with confirmed bookings to another hotel when no room is available), compensation and legal duties; these vary by country. Distribution channels include direct booking, online travel agencies (OTAs), global distribution systems (booking systems used by travel agents) and wholesalers. Each channel has a cost of acquisition, and rate parity rules may limit price differences. Channel management compares net revenue, not just gross rate.

sections.heading: Systems and data
sections.text: A property management system (PMS) records reservations, rates, occupancy and guest accounts. A revenue management system (RMS) uses that data to forecast demand and recommend prices and inventory controls. Good output depends on clean data, correct segmentation and human judgement. Systems support decisions; they do not replace an understanding of the market.

keyPoints: Perishability means an unsold room night cannot be stored and sold later.
Forecast demand by date, segment and rate using booking pace, seasonality and local events.
Occupancy = rooms sold ÷ rooms available; ADR = room revenue ÷ rooms sold; RevPAR = room revenue ÷ rooms available = ADR × occupancy.
Rate fencing uses conditions such as advance purchase and non-refundable terms to separate segments.
Yield management allocates rooms across segments and rates to maximise contribution, not occupancy alone.
Overbooking uses expected no-shows = bookings × no-show rate and needs a clear walk policy; PMS records data while an RMS recommends controls.

en.title: Hospitality Financial Management
en.short: Budgets, ratios, menu costing, cash flow and investment appraisal for hotels and restaurants.

sections.heading: Budgets and variances
sections.text: A budget is a financial plan for a period, usually a year, set by departments. Variance analysis compares actual results with the budget. A variance is favourable if profit is higher or cost lower than planned, and unfavourable if the reverse. Managers should separate price and volume effects, because a cost overrun may come from higher prices or from using more inputs. Flexible budgets adjust for actual sales volume, so comparisons are fair.

sections.heading: Operating ratios
sections.text: Occupancy percentage = rooms sold ÷ rooms available × 100. Food cost percentage = food cost ÷ food sales × 100. Labour cost percentage = labour cost ÷ total revenue × 100. Gross operating profit (GOP) is revenue minus departmental expenses and undistributed operating expenses (overheads such as admin, marketing and utilities), before rent, tax, interest and depreciation. GOP margin = GOP ÷ revenue × 100. These ratios show where costs are out of line, but compare like with like: a luxury hotel and a budget hotel have different normal ratios.

sections.heading: Menu costing and cash
sections.text: Menu costing adds ingredient cost and an allowance for waste. If a dish costs 4.00 to make and the target food cost percentage is 30%, price = 4.00 ÷ 0.30 = 13.33. Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. Hotels hold cash, food and receivables, so a cash flow forecast lists expected receipts and payments month by month. It warns of shortages even when the business is profitable.

sections.heading: Investment appraisal
sections.text: Payback is the time to recover the initial outlay. Net present value (NPV) discounts future cash flows at a required rate and subtracts the outlay. Internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate that makes NPV zero. A project costing 100,000 with inflows of 40,000 for four years has payback = 100,000 ÷ 40,000 = 2.5 years. At 10%, the four-year annuity factor (the present value of 1 a year for four years) is 3.1699, so NPV = 40,000 × 3.1699 − 100,000 = 26,796. IRR is about 22%. Accept if NPV is positive or IRR exceeds the required rate.

keyPoints: Variance = actual − budget; label it favourable or unfavourable by its effect on profit.
Occupancy = rooms sold ÷ rooms available × 100; food cost percentage = food cost ÷ food sales × 100.
GOP = revenue − departmental and undistributed operating expenses, before rent, tax, interest and depreciation.
Menu price = ingredient cost ÷ target food cost percentage.
Working capital = current assets − current liabilities; cash flow forecasts show timing, not just profit.
For equal annual inflows, payback = initial outlay ÷ annual cash inflow; accept a project if NPV is positive or IRR exceeds the required rate.

en.title: Human Resource Management in Hospitality
en.short: It covers recruitment, training, motivation, turnover, scheduling, law and seasonal staffing in hospitality.

sections.heading: Recruitment and induction
sections.text: Human resource management (HRM) is the planned management of people at work. Recruitment starts with job analysis, producing a job description (duties) and person specification (skills and attitude). Hospitality firms recruit internally through promotion and externally through job boards, agencies, schools and referrals. Selection uses structured interviews, work samples, references and right-to-work checks. Induction is the first orientation: it explains the property, team, service standards, safety and pay. Weak induction raises early leaving.

sections.heading: Training and reward
sections.text: Training builds skills for the current job; development prepares people for wider roles. Hospitality uses on-the-job coaching, off-the-job courses, cross-training and statutory training. Motivation is the drive to act. Reward includes pay, tips or service charge, benefits, recognition and promotion. Tips and service charge rules vary by country, so distribute them transparently. Herzberg’s motivators and hygiene factors help: fair pay prevents dissatisfaction, while achievement encourages effort. Reward must be legal and explained.

sections.heading: Turnover and scheduling
sections.text: Labour turnover is the rate at which staff leave and are replaced. Turnover = leavers in a year ÷ average number of staff × 100. Retention means keeping good people through realistic recruitment, good induction, development, fair shifts and recognition. Scheduling matches staff to forecast demand. Labour cost percentage = labour cost ÷ revenue × 100. If monthly labour cost is ₦2,400,000 and revenue is ₦8,000,000, the ratio is 30%. Managers control it by forecasting, flexible shifts, cross-training and overtime control.

sections.heading: Law and diversity
sections.text: Employment law sets minimum terms, dismissal rules, equality, health and safety and union rights. In Nigeria, the Labour Act covers core terms for many workers; in the UK, the Employment Rights Act 1996 and Equality Act 2010 apply. Details differ, so check official sources. A diverse workforce includes ages, genders, nationalities and abilities. Manage it with fair recruitment, inclusion training and anti-harassment rules. Seasonal workers need clear contracts, induction, safe rotas and fair treatment; a core plus flexible team helps.

keyPoints: Recruitment uses job analysis, a job description and a person specification; selection should use structured interviews and work samples.
Induction and training reduce early leaving and build service skills.
Reward must be legal, transparent and linked to motivation, not only pay.
Labour turnover = leavers in a year ÷ average number of staff × 100.
Labour cost percentage = labour cost ÷ revenue × 100.
Employment law differs by country, so check current official rules; seasonal and diverse staff need fair, clear treatment.

en.title: Hospitality and Tourism Law
en.short: Guest contracts, innkeeper’s duty and lien, safety, food licensing, consumer, travel and data rules.

sections.heading: Contract and lien
sections.text:
A booking is usually a contract. The guest offers, the hotel accepts, and payment is consideration, meaning something of value given in exchange. The booking terms form part of it. Many common law countries recognise an innkeeper’s duty to receive travellers without reasonable excuse, but statutes differ. An innkeeper’s lien is a common law right to keep a guest’s property until unpaid charges are paid. It does not permit detention of the guest. Some countries limit it by statute.

Example: Ada books a room in Lagos and pays a deposit. The hotel must provide the room on the agreed terms. If she cancels, any refund depends on the contract and consumer law. If she leaves without paying, the hotel may claim the debt and, where local law allows, use a lien over her luggage. It must not detain her.

sections.heading: Safety and food
sections.text: Hotels owe guests a duty of care. They must take reasonable steps to prevent foreseeable harm: secure locks, fire precautions, safe premises and trained staff. Occupiers’ liability statutes in jurisdictions such as England and Wales set standards. Food safety is separate: kitchens need registration or licensing and inspection by the relevant authority, and staff must follow hygiene rules. Requirements vary by country and city.

sections.heading: Consumers and travel
sections.text: Consumer protection law gives guests remedies for misleading descriptions, unfair terms and unsafe services. In Nigeria, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018 established the FCCPC. Travel sellers may need a licence. In England and Wales, the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018 require organisers of package holidays to provide information and insolvency protection.

sections.heading: Data protection
sections.text: Data protection limits what hotels do with guest data. A hotel is usually a data controller, the party that decides how personal data is used. It must collect only what it needs, keep it secure and respect access rights. The EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies in the EU, and Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 applies in Nigeria. Rules differ, so name the jurisdiction.

keyPoints: A hotel booking is generally a contract on the booking terms.
An innkeeper’s lien lets a hotel keep a guest’s property for unpaid charges, not detain the guest.
Hotels owe a duty of care for guest safety and security.
Food businesses need registration or licensing and inspection.
Package travel rules and consumer law vary by country, so name the jurisdiction.
Data protection limits collection, use and storage of guest data.

en.title: Food and Beverage Management
en.short: Menu engineering, purchasing, standard recipes, cost control, HACCP and service standards.

sections.heading: Menu engineering and pricing
sections.text:
Menu engineering classifies dishes by popularity and contribution margin (selling price minus food cost). Stars are popular and profitable; plowhorses are popular but low margin; puzzles are unpopular but high margin; dogs are low on both. Thresholds vary by outlet.

Pricing often uses food cost percentage: food cost ÷ selling price × 100. If a portion costs 2,400 naira and sells for 8,000 naira:
food cost percentage = 2,400 ÷ 8,000 = 30%
contribution margin = 8,000 − 2,400 = 5,600 naira
To hit 30%, price = 2,400 ÷ 0.30 = 8,000 naira.
Check: 2,400 ÷ 8,000 = 0.30.

sections.heading: Purchasing and production
sections.text:
Purchasing begins with a purchase specification: a written description of an item’s quality, size, grade, packaging and delivery conditions. It lets buyers compare suppliers and reject substandard goods. Inventory control sets par stock (the standard level to hold), reorder points and stock counts. First in, first out (FIFO) reduces spoilage. Stock turnover = cost of food used ÷ average stock value.

Production planning matches forecast demand with staff, equipment and preparation time. A standard recipe states ingredients, quantities, yield, portion size and method. It makes costing and consistency possible. If a recipe yields 20 portions and costs 60,000 naira in total, cost per portion is 60,000 ÷ 20 = 3,000 naira.

sections.heading: Labour, overhead and safety
sections.text:
Labour cost percentage = labour cost ÷ sales × 100. Managers compare it with budget and with sales per labour hour. Overhead control covers energy, water, waste and administration.

HACCP (Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point) is a preventive food safety system with seven principles: identify hazards; determine critical control points (CCPs); set critical limits; monitor CCPs; take corrective action; verify; keep records. Prerequisite programmes such as cleaning support it. Food safety rules differ by country, so check the local authority.

sections.heading: Quality and service standards
sections.text:
Quality and service standards define what the outlet promises: food quality, speed, cleanliness, staff knowledge and atmosphere. Standards must be realistic and reviewed.

Written standards, checklists, training, guest feedback and mystery visits help managers measure performance. Good service is consistent, not merely friendly on one day.

keyPoints: Food cost percentage = food cost ÷ selling price × 100.
Contribution margin = selling price − food cost.
Stock turnover = cost of food used ÷ average stock value.
Labour cost percentage = labour cost ÷ sales × 100.
HACCP has seven principles and is supported by prerequisite programmes.
Service standards must be written, trained, measured and reviewed.

en.title: Tour operations and the travel trade
en.short: Travel agents, tour operators, package pricing, GDS, IATA ticketing, documents and online booking.

sections.heading: Roles in the trade
sections.text: Travel agents sell travel products for suppliers and advise clients, earning commission or fees. Tour operators assemble packages, often buying accommodation in blocks and taking commercial risk. Consolidators buy seats in bulk at negotiated fares and resell them, usually through agents. Roles overlap: an online travel agency (OTA) is a website retailer. Licensing and bonding rules differ by country; bonding is a financial guarantee that protects customers if the firm fails. Check the local authority.

sections.heading: Building and pricing packages
sections.text: A package combines transport, accommodation and often transfers or activities into one price. The operator estimates demand, contracts capacity, sets a price and bears the risk of unsold places. Price must cover direct costs, overheads and profit. Example: hotel 40,000 per night for two nights, return transport 30,000 and transfer 5,000. Direct cost = 40,000 × 2 + 30,000 + 5,000 = 115,000. Add 15% markup: 115,000 × 1.15 = 132,250. Check markup = 17,250, which is 15% of 115,000. Unsold contracted places remain a cost unless contracts allow release (returning unsold places to the supplier by an agreed date).

sections.heading: Distribution and ticketing
sections.text: A global distribution system (GDS) is a network that lets agents compare and book airline seats, hotel rooms and car rentals. Airlines also sell through their websites, OTAs and call centres. IATA, the International Air Transport Association, runs accreditation and settlement for agents in many countries, often through a Billing and Settlement Plan (BSP). Rules vary, so check IATA and the local authority. An e-ticket is an electronic record with a ticket number and itinerary; fare rules set change, cancellation and baggage conditions. A passenger name record (PNR) holds the booking, not the ticket.

sections.heading: Documents and online booking
sections.text: Travel documents include a passport, visas, health certificates and, where required, proof of onward travel. Validity rules differ by destination and nationality; check the embassy or official government source. Online booking has shifted leisure retail to airline sites and OTAs. This disintermediation (cutting out the traditional agent) reduced agents’ ticket sales, while many agents now focus on complex itineraries, corporate travel, groups and advice. Tour operators add value through packaging and risk management.

keyPoints: Travel agents retail travel and advise; tour operators assemble packages and carry unsold-capacity risk.
Consolidators buy bulk seats at negotiated fares and resell, usually through agents.
Package selling price = direct cost + overheads + profit; markup is profit on cost, margin is profit on price.
A GDS lets agents book airline, hotel and car inventory; IATA accreditation and BSP settlement rules vary by country.
An e-ticket is the ticket record; a PNR is the booking file, not the ticket.
Online booking caused disintermediation, but agents and operators remain for complex, packaged and corporate travel.

en.title: Events Management: Design, Delivery and Legacy
en.short: Event design, feasibility, budgets, venues, risk, sponsorship, marketing and legacy.

sections.heading: Design and feasibility
sections.text: Event design sets the purpose, audience, format and experience of an event. A feasibility study tests whether the idea can work: demand, venue capacity, costs, income, permissions and risk. It should come before heavy spending. Objectives must be measurable, such as attendance, income or learning outcomes.

sections.heading: Planning and budgeting
sections.text:
Planning turns the concept into tasks, deadlines and responsibilities. A run sheet lists what happens, when and who is responsible. Budgeting separates fixed costs, which do not change with attendance, from variable costs, which rise per guest. Break-even attendance is fixed costs divided by the contribution per ticket, meaning ticket price minus variable cost per attendee.

Illustrative example in naira: fixed costs 3,000,000; variable cost 900 per attendee; ticket price 2,500. Contribution = 2,500 − 900 = 1,600. Break-even = 3,000,000 ÷ 1,600 = 1,875 attendees. At 2,000 attendees, profit = (2,000 × 1,600) − 3,000,000 = 200,000.

sections.heading: Venue, logistics and risk
sections.text: Venue selection compares capacity, location, access, technical facilities, cost and licensing. Logistics covers the flow of people, suppliers, equipment and waste. A risk assessment identifies hazards, likelihood and impact, then sets controls. Safety planning includes emergency exits, first aid, insurance, security and crowd management. Crowd management uses entry control, spacing and clear communication to prevent crushing. Rules differ by country, so check local permits and fire regulations.

sections.heading: Sponsorship, marketing and legacy
sections.text: Sponsorship is cash or in-kind support given in return for audience access and brand exposure. Marketing uses the marketing mix: product, price, place and promotion, with people, process and physical evidence added for services such as events. Evaluation compares attendance, income and spending with the plan, and gathers feedback. Legacy is the lasting economic, social or environmental effect after the event, such as skills, facilities or destination reputation.

keyPoints: A feasibility study tests demand, costs, capacity, permissions and risk before major spending.
A run sheet turns the plan into timed tasks and named responsibilities.
Break-even attendance = fixed costs ÷ (ticket price − variable cost per attendee).
Venue choice must match capacity, access, technical needs, cost and local licensing.
Risk assessment identifies hazards, likelihood and impact, then sets controls; crowd management needs entry control, spacing and clear communication.
Evaluation compares results with the plan, and legacy is the lasting effect after the event.

en.title: Tourism Planning and Policy
en.short: National, regional and local planning, policy tools, carrying capacity, stakeholders and development models.

sections.heading: Three planning levels
sections.text: Tourism planning sets goals and actions. National planning covers laws, visas, marketing and major infrastructure. Regional planning coordinates a province or coast, such as transport and protected areas. Local planning handles zoning, signage, waste, access and community benefits. Levels must agree: a national growth target fails if local water and roads cannot cope. The cycle is assess resources and demand, set objectives, choose strategies, consult, implement, monitor, revise.

sections.heading: Instruments and stakeholders
sections.text:
Policy instruments are government tools. Regulation sets rules: hotel licensing, heritage protection or limits on new buildings. Incentives are carrots: tax relief, grants or cheap land for training and rural projects. Marketing promotes the destination, often by a national tourism board. Public investment and information are also instruments. A consistent mix matters; marketing cannot repair poor regulation.

Stakeholders include residents, businesses, workers, visitors, NGOs and cultural groups. Participation means involving them in decisions, not just informing them. It builds trust and local knowledge, but needs time and clear rules so loud groups do not dominate.

sections.heading: Carrying capacity
sections.text:
Carrying capacity is the visitor use an area can absorb before unacceptable change. It has physical, ecological, social and infrastructure dimensions. Visitor management turns capacity into action: entry limits, timed tickets, zoning, fees, shuttle buses and codes of conduct.

Example: a beach can take 500 visitors a day without damage, but peak demand is 800. The excess is 800 − 500 = 300. Managers could cap entries at 500, spread demand with off-peak pricing, or raise the limit by improving facilities. The figure is a judgement; monitor and revise.

sections.heading: Development models
sections.text: Models guide choices. Master planning sets a long-term framework. Community-based tourism gives residents ownership and benefits. Tourism area life cycle describes destinations moving through stages from exploration and involvement to development, consolidation and stagnation, then decline or rejuvenation. In Namibia, community conservancies link tourism, wildlife and local income. Costa Rica uses parks and ecotourism. Barcelona limits accommodation and taxes visitors. Models must fit context; results vary.

keyPoints: Tourism planning works at national, regional and local levels, and the levels must agree.
Policy instruments include regulation, incentives, marketing, public investment and information.
Carrying capacity is the use an area can absorb before unacceptable change; it is a judgement, not a fixed number.
Visitor management uses limits, pricing, zoning and facilities to keep use within capacity.
Stakeholder participation improves decisions but needs time and clear rules.
Development models such as master planning, community-based tourism and the tourism area life cycle must fit local context.

en.title: Sustainable Tourism
en.short: Economic, social and environmental impacts, climate, certification, community tourism and visitor management.

sections.heading: Impacts and triple bottom line
sections.text:
Sustainable tourism seeks tourism’s benefits while limiting harm. Economic impacts include income, jobs and foreign exchange, but leakages occur when money leaves for imports or foreign owners. Socio-cultural impacts include cultural pride and exchange, but also crowding, commercialisation and loss of local control. Environmental impacts include conservation revenue, but also energy and water use, waste, habitat damage and wildlife disturbance.

The triple bottom line, linked to John Elkington, asks managers to report profit (economic), people (socio-cultural) and planet (environmental). Good performance on one line does not excuse damage on another.

sections.heading: Climate and certification
sections.text:
Climate change and tourism interact. Tourism emits greenhouse gases, mainly from transport and building energy. Destinations face heatwaves, water shortages, coastal erosion and coral bleaching, affecting attractions and safety. Adaptation prepares for these risks; mitigation reduces emissions.

Certification is a voluntary label from an independent body after assessment. A standard sets the criteria. The Global Sustainable Tourism Council (GSTC) publishes widely used criteria, and ISO 14001 is an environmental management standard. Certification can guide buyers, but weak audits allow greenwashing: claiming more environmental virtue than exists.

sections.heading: Community and pro-poor tourism
sections.text:
Community-based tourism (CBT) gives local people ownership or strong control of tourism enterprises. Pro-poor tourism (PPT) is a wider approach seeking net benefits for poor people through jobs, supply chains or community fees. Neither is automatically fair; elite capture (local elites taking the benefits) and unequal wages can occur.

Case: a made-up village, Mbawe, beside a wildlife area, opens a campsite owned by a community trust. It trains local guides, buys food locally and pays a fee to a conservation fund. The test is whether profits, decisions and costs are shared fairly, not simply whether visitors arrive.

sections.heading: Visitor management
sections.text: Responsible visitor management controls numbers, timing and behaviour. Carrying capacity is the use an area can absorb before unacceptable ecological or social damage. Tools include zoning, permits, timed entry, differential pricing, guided routes, codes of conduct and monitoring. Managers should set limits from evidence and review them as seasons and infrastructure change.

keyPoints: Sustainable tourism balances economic, socio-cultural and environmental outcomes, often summarised by the triple bottom line.
Tourism causes leakages, cultural change and environmental pressure as well as benefits.
Tourism both contributes to climate change and must adapt to its effects.
Certification is voluntary and depends on credible standards and audits; GSTC criteria and ISO 14001 are examples.
Community-based tourism stresses local control, while pro-poor tourism stresses net benefits to poor people.
Visitor management uses carrying capacity, zoning, permits, pricing and monitoring to limit harm.

en.title: Tourism Economics: Demand, Multipliers and Measurement
en.short: Tourism demand, elasticity, multipliers, satellite accounts and balance of payments effects.

sections.heading: Demand and elasticity
sections.text: Tourism demand is the travel and related services people are willing and able to buy at a given price and time. It is composite demand: transport, accommodation, food and attractions. Price elasticity = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price. Income elasticity uses income instead. Cross elasticity compares quantity with the price of a substitute or complement. An absolute value above 1 is elastic; below 1 is inelastic. Demand also depends on exchange rates, safety and seasonality.

sections.heading: Multiplier and leakage
sections.text: Tourist spending becomes income for hotels, staff and suppliers, who spend again. The simple multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 − c), where c is the share of extra income spent locally. Leakages leave the local economy: imports, taxes, profits sent abroad and savings. If c = 0.6, the multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5. Extra visitor spending of 1,000,000 supports 2,500,000 of local income in this model. Capacity limits usually make the real effect smaller.

sections.heading: Measuring tourism
sections.text: A tourism satellite account (TSA) is a statistical framework, linked to the System of National Accounts, that measures tourism consumption, tourism industries, direct gross value added, direct GDP and employment. It shows direct effects only; indirect and induced effects need separate models. The balance of payments records inbound visitor spending as a services export credit and outbound spending as a debit. Currency depreciation can improve price competitiveness for foreign visitors but raises import costs. The real exchange rate adjusts for inflation.

sections.heading: Economic contribution
sections.text: Tourism’s contribution is often reported as direct, indirect and induced. Direct comes from visitor spending in tourism industries. Indirect comes through supply chains. Induced comes when employees spend wages. For a made-up country, 500,000 inbound visitors each spend US$800. Receipts = 500,000 × 800 = US$400,000,000. If 35% leaks to imports, retained spending = 400,000,000 × 0.65 = US$260,000,000. This is spending, not value added, so it is not tourism GDP.

keyPoints: Price elasticity = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price, and income elasticity uses income instead.
The simple tourism multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 − c), where c is the share of extra income spent locally.
Leakages include imports, taxes, profits sent abroad and savings.
A tourism satellite account measures tourism’s direct contribution within the national accounts and is not a separate GDP.
In the balance of payments, inbound visitor spending is a services export credit and outbound spending is a debit.
Currency depreciation can improve inbound price competitiveness but raises import costs.

en.title: Cultural and Heritage Tourism
en.short: Culture, heritage, authenticity, interpretation, museums, festivals and conservation at cultural sites.

sections.heading: Culture and heritage
sections.text: Culture is a group’s learned, shared way of life: beliefs, values, customs, arts and language. Heritage is what a society inherits from the past and chooses to pass on, including monuments, objects, landscapes and living practices. Cultural tourism is travel motivated by culture; heritage tourism is visiting heritage places. Heritage is not only the past: each generation selects and contests it. In Africa, heritage includes rock art, palaces, sacred groves and oral traditions. Sites may be valued locally for worship and nationally for tourism.

sections.heading: Authenticity and interpretation
sections.text: Authenticity debates ask whether a tourist experience is genuine. Objectivists look for original material and unchanged practice. Constructivists say authenticity is negotiated and changes with context. Existentialists ask whether the visitor feels true to themselves. MacCannell called staged authenticity the front-stage performance that hides back-stage life. Interpretation explains a site’s meanings and relationships, not just facts. Guides, labels, storytelling and accessible routes shape the visitor experience. Robben Island Museum in South Africa uses guided tours, often led by former political prisoners, to connect the prison to apartheid and freedom.

sections.heading: Museums, festivals and intangible heritage
sections.text: Museums collect, preserve, research and exhibit objects, but they also interpret. Festivals turn heritage into performance and can strengthen identity and income. UNESCO’s 2003 Convention protects intangible heritage: oral traditions, performing arts, rituals, festive events, crafts and knowledge. Ifá divination is a Nigerian practice inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The Osun-Osogbo festival in Nigeria is linked to a sacred grove that is also a World Heritage site. Tourism can support these practices, but commerce may simplify them.

sections.heading: Conservation and management
sections.text: Cultural destinations face a tension between access and preservation. Managers use visitor limits, timed entry, protective walkways, monitoring and maintenance. They need community consent, benefit sharing, training and rules against looting and illegal trade. Great Zimbabwe, a stone-built city in Zimbabwe, needs vegetation control, path management and careful presentation of its history. Tourism income can fund conservation if fees are retained and planned for. Without local involvement, conservation can feel like exclusion.

keyPoints: Culture is a shared way of life; heritage is what a society inherits and chooses to pass on.
Authenticity can be judged by original material, by negotiated meaning or by visitor feeling.
Interpretation reveals meanings and relationships, not only facts.
Museums and festivals present heritage, while UNESCO’s 2003 Convention protects intangible heritage.
African examples include Robben Island, Ifá divination, Osun-Osogbo and Great Zimbabwe.
Conservation must balance access, preservation and community benefit.

en.title: Hospitality Information Technology
en.short: PMS, CRS and GDS, OTAs, channel managers, guest tech, card security and operational data.

sections.heading: Core systems
sections.text: A property management system (PMS) is the main software at one hotel. It handles reservations, room status, guest folios, billing and housekeeping lists. A central reservation system (CRS) holds room inventory and rates for a chain or group and sends them to sales channels. A global distribution system (GDS) is a network that travel agents use to book flights, hotels and other services; Amadeus, Sabre and Travelport are GDS companies. Data flows from PMS to CRS to GDS and other channels, so a room sold once should disappear everywhere.

sections.heading: Distribution channels
sections.text: An online travel agency (OTA), such as Booking.com or Expedia, sells rooms and charges commission. A channel manager is software that links the PMS or CRS to OTAs and other channels. It updates rates and availability in near real time and closes a date when the last room is sold. Without it, staff must update each OTA site by hand, and overbooking or rate mismatch becomes likely. Direct bookings through the hotel website reduce commission but still need the same inventory control.

sections.heading: Guest technology and security
sections.text: Guest-facing technology includes self-service kiosks, mobile check-in and digital keys, in-room tablets, Wi-Fi portals and chatbots. Each collects personal data, so access should be limited, devices patched, traffic encrypted and backups tested. Payment card data is governed by the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), an industry standard rather than a law. Tokenisation replaces card numbers with a token. Data protection laws differ by country; Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 applies in Nigeria.

sections.heading: Data for decisions
sections.text: Operational data supports daily choices: occupancy forecast for staffing, check-out counts for housekeeping, maintenance logs for repairs and guest feedback for service recovery. Example: a 200-room hotel forecasts 80% occupancy, so 160 rooms are occupied. If 70 rooms check out and 90 stay over, housekeeping must service 160 rooms. At 14 rooms per attendant per shift, 160 ÷ 14 = 11.43, so 12 attendants are needed. Forecasts are estimates, so managers keep a buffer.

keyPoints: A PMS runs one property; a CRS holds chain inventory; a GDS connects travel agents to suppliers.
A channel manager keeps rates and availability aligned across OTAs and direct channels.
OTAs charge commission, so direct bookings can save money but need the same inventory control.
Guest-facing technology collects personal data, so access control, encryption and staff training are essential.
PCI DSS is an industry card-data standard, not a law; data protection laws vary by country.
Rooms to service = check-outs + stayovers; attendants needed = rooms to service ÷ rooms cleaned per attendant.

en.title: Entrepreneurship in Hospitality and Tourism
en.short: Spotting opportunities, choosing a business model, planning, funding and franchising small tourism ventures.

sections.heading: Spotting opportunities
sections.text: Opportunity recognition means finding a real gap that customers will pay to fill. Look for visitor flows, complaints, missing services and local skills. A tour guide may notice that birdwatchers lack transport; a cook may see demand for packed lunches. Test the idea with a few paying guests before investing. Ask who the customer is, why they will choose you, what you must offer and whether the numbers can work. Demand in tourism is seasonal and depends on the destination’s reputation, so check both.

sections.heading: Business models
sections.text: A business model explains how a venture creates, delivers and captures value. A small hotel or guesthouse earns from rooms and extras; occupancy (rooms sold as a share of rooms available) and average room rate drive income. A tour guide may charge per tour, sell packages or earn commission from partners. Food service can use a fixed menu, events or delivery. Keep the model simple, price for full costs, and protect cash flow. A made-up case: Amina runs a four-room guesthouse in Cape Coast, Ghana. She adds guided walks and breakfast, which raise income without new rooms.

sections.heading: Plan and finance
sections.text: A business plan sets out the idea, market, operations, team, marketing, risks and financial forecasts. It is for you and for lenders or investors. Sources of finance include savings, family, microfinance (small loans), bank loans, grants, angel investors (wealthy individuals who invest in early ventures), venture capital and crowdfunding. Availability and rules differ by country, so check local agencies and current terms. Loans need repayment; equity investors take ownership. Forecast cash monthly, because tourism income is uneven.

sections.heading: Franchising and risks
sections.text: Franchising is a licence to use a brand and system. The franchisor supplies standards and support; the franchisee pays fees and royalties (ongoing payments) and follows rules. It can reduce risk for a new operator but limits independence. Small tourism businesses face seasonality, thin margins, high fixed costs, staff turnover, weak infrastructure, regulation and competition from online platforms. Keep reserves, diversify income and join local networks.

keyPoints: Opportunity recognition starts with a customer problem or missing service that visitors will pay for.
A business model shows how a venture creates, delivers and captures value.
Small hotels earn from rooms and extras; guides and food services can combine fees, packages and commissions.
A business plan explains the market, operations, team, risks and cash forecasts.
Finance can come from savings, loans, grants or equity, but terms and availability vary by country.
Franchising gives a brand and system for fees and royalties, but reduces independence.

en.title: Research Methods in Hospitality and Tourism
en.short: Research questions, designs, sampling, tools, analysis, ethics and report writing.

sections.heading: Question and design
sections.text:
A research question states exactly what you will answer. It should be narrow, answerable and linked to a gap in existing knowledge. A good question might ask how room attendants in Accra perceive workload, not whether hospitality is important.

Research design is the plan for collecting evidence. A survey collects standard answers from many people. A case study examines one bounded unit, such as a hotel, in depth. Interviews give rich accounts. Observation records behaviour directly. Choose the design that fits the question, not the one that seems easiest.

sections.heading: Sampling and tools
sections.text:
Sampling is selecting part of a population, the full group you study. A sampling frame is a list of that group. Probability sampling gives everyone a known chance; simple random and systematic sampling are examples. Non-probability sampling, such as convenience sampling, is quicker but limits generalisation.

Case: a student studies 600 past guests of a hotel in Accra, Ghana. Using systematic sampling, the student picks every fifth name. The sample is 600 ÷ 5 = 120 guests.

A questionnaire needs clear, neutral questions, one idea per item, and a pilot test. An interview guide lists themes and probes, not a rigid script.

sections.heading: Analysis and ethics
sections.text:
Quantitative analysis turns numbers into descriptive statistics, such as frequencies, means and cross-tabulations. Qualitative analysis often uses coding: labelling text, then grouping labels into themes. Do not claim that a small convenience sample represents all guests.

Ethics protect people. Seek informed consent, explain the purpose, keep data confidential, avoid harm, and obtain institutional approval. Anonymity means you cannot identify a person; confidentiality means you know but do not disclose.

sections.heading: Writing the report
sections.text: A dissertation or project report usually has introduction, literature review, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and references. The methods chapter explains and justifies your choices. The discussion links findings to the literature and states limitations. Write plainly, keep an audit trail of decisions, and reference every source. Check your institution’s rules on length, format and ethics approval.

keyPoints: A research question should be narrow, answerable and linked to a gap in knowledge.
Research design is the plan for collecting evidence; survey, case study, interview and observation answer different questions.
Probability sampling gives every member a known chance; non-probability sampling limits generalisation.
Systematic sample size = population ÷ sampling interval.
Quantitative analysis summarises numbers; qualitative analysis codes text into themes.
Ethics require informed consent, confidentiality, no harm and approval; the report must justify methods and state limitations.

en.title: Ethics and Professional Practice
en.short: Ethical issues, CSR, professional codes and managers’ duties to guests, staff and communities.

sections.heading: Ethical issues
sections.text: Ethics is the study of what is right and wrong, and professional practice is the conduct expected of someone who holds specialist knowledge and public trust. In hospitality and tourism, pricing can mislead guests through hidden charges or surge prices that are not explained. Tipping is ethical when it rewards service and is transparent, but it can become unfair if managers use it to replace a living wage. Labour practices raise questions about long hours, insecure contracts, child labour and migrant workers. Sexual exploitation, including child sex tourism, is a crime and never a service. Cultural respect means presenting local people and traditions honestly, not as curiosities. Environmental duty means reducing waste, water and energy use and protecting places that visitors come to see.

sections.heading: Responsibility and codes
sections.text: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) is a firm’s voluntary duty to consider its effects on staff, guests, communities and the environment beyond legal minimums. It can include fair recruitment, local sourcing, accessible facilities and honest reporting. Professional codes set out expected conduct. The UN Tourism Global Code of Ethics for Tourism, adopted in 1999, is an international framework. National bodies also issue codes; examples include the Institute of Hospitality in the UK and the American Hotel & Lodging Association in the US. Managers owe guests safety, privacy and truthful information; staff fair pay, dignity and safe conditions; and communities respect for land, culture and local benefit. When duties conflict, managers should record the decision, consult those affected and follow the law.

sections.heading: Case: coastal lodge
sections.text: At a made-up coastal lodge in Ghana, the manager finds that guides are paid only by tips and that a tour visits a village without consent. She moves guides to a guaranteed wage, explains tipping in booking materials, agrees a fee and visiting rules with elders, and sets a water-saving target.
