She records the changes and reports them to owners and guests. The lodge earns less per booking, but staff turnover falls and community trust grows.

keyPoints: Ethics asks what is right; professional practice is the conduct expected of a trusted specialist.
Pricing and tipping must be transparent and must not hide the true cost of service or replace fair wages.
Sexual exploitation, including child sex tourism, is a crime and never an acceptable service.
CSR is voluntary action beyond legal minimums towards staff, guests, communities and the environment.
Codes such as the UN Tourism Global Code of Ethics for Tourism guide conduct, but national law and local rules still apply.
Managers balance duties to guests, staff and communities by consulting, recording decisions and following the law.

en.title: Strategic Management in Hospitality and Tourism
en.short: Competitive analysis, growth, branding, franchising, mergers and multi-unit strategy implementation.

sections.heading: Competitive analysis
sections.text:
Porter’s five forces judges industry attractiveness: rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, buyer power and supplier power. In hotels, high fixed costs can intensify rivalry, and online travel agencies can raise buyer power.

The resource-based view (RBV) looks inside the firm. It asks whether resources are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and supported by the organisation (VRIO). A rival can buy another good site, but a service culture and reputation are much harder to copy. Five forces explains the industry; RBV explains why one firm outperforms another.

sections.heading: Growth and internationalisation
sections.text:
Growth can follow Ansoff’s matrix: market penetration, product development, market development and diversification. A hotel may penetrate an existing city, add conference products, enter a new country or diversify into restaurants.

Internationalisation adds currency, legal, labour and cultural risk. Firms often enter through management contracts, where the owner keeps the asset and pays an operator fee, or franchises, which need less capital but weaken direct control. The choice depends on capabilities and local knowledge.

sections.heading: Brands, franchising and deals
sections.text:
A brand is a promise of consistent quality; brand equity is the value customers attach to it. Franchising is a contract in which the franchisor licenses its brand and systems to a franchisee for fees and royalties. It enables fast growth with less capital, but weak franchisees can damage the brand.

Mergers and acquisitions (M&A) combine firms or buy control. They can create synergies (combined gains), but fail when due diligence misses debt, culture clashes or integration costs. A made-up group, Adunni Hotels, buys a rival with eight hotels; it must merge booking systems and retrain staff.

sections.heading: Implementation across units
sections.text:
Strategy implementation turns plans into action across units. Multi-unit hotel and tourism businesses need standard operating procedures, budgets, staff incentives and audits.

They also need local adaptation: a city hotel and a beach resort cannot use identical staffing. A useful test is alignment: do structure, rewards and information systems support the chosen strategy? If not, the strategy stalls.

keyPoints: Porter’s five forces assesses rivalry, entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power.
The resource-based view tests resources for value, rarity, imitability and organisational support.
Ansoff’s matrix sets out penetration, product development, market development and diversification.
Franchising and management contracts allow growth with less capital but reduce direct control.
Mergers and acquisitions can create synergies, but integration and due diligence risks are high.
Multi-unit strategy needs standard procedures, local adaptation and aligned incentives.

en.title: Advanced Tourism Theory
en.short: Mobilities, the tourist gaze, postmodern and critical turns, systems, authenticity and experience.

sections.heading: Mobilities and the gaze
sections.text: The mobilities paradigm, associated with John Urry and Mimi Sheller, treats tourism as one part of wider flows of people, objects, images and information. It asks how travel, migration, media and transport connect, rather than studying a holiday in isolation. The tourist gaze, also from Urry, means the socially organised way visitors look at places and people. Expectations are shaped by guidebooks, photographs and status. Later work notes that tourism is also embodied and performed, and that hosts gaze back. So the visual is important but not the whole story.

sections.heading: Postmodern and critical turns
sections.text: Postmodern tourism studies stress spectacle, pastiche (mixing styles) and blurred boundaries between home and away. Places may be staged for images, and copies can feel more real than originals, a condition called hyperreality. Critical tourism studies ask who holds power, who labours, who is represented and who gains. They examine colonialism, class, gender and inequality in tourism. The two schools overlap, but postmodern work often reads culture and meaning, while critical work foregrounds political economy and justice. A student should compare their questions, not choose one as final.

sections.heading: Systems, complexity and authenticity
sections.text: Systems approaches model tourism as interacting parts, such as demand, supply, transport, destinations and governance, with feedback. Complexity approaches add non-linearity, emergence and uncertainty: small changes can produce large effects, and destinations adapt. Authenticity debates ask what makes an experience genuine. Objective views value original objects; constructivist views say authenticity is negotiated and invented; existential views focus on the visitor’s felt meaning. Experience economy work studies staged memorable experiences. Consider Ama, a diaspora visitor touring a community heritage village near Kumasi. Mobilities asks how migration and social media shape her trip. The gaze asks what she expects. Critical studies ask who earns and who scripts the dance. Authenticity asks whether she values origin, construction or feeling. The lenses answer different questions.

keyPoints: The mobilities paradigm places tourism within wider flows of people, objects, images and information.
The tourist gaze is socially organised, so what visitors notice depends on expectations and status.
Postmodern tourism studies emphasise spectacle, hyperreality and blurred boundaries.
Critical tourism studies examine power, labour, representation and inequality.
Systems and complexity approaches treat tourism as interacting, adaptive and uncertain.
Authenticity may be judged by original objects, social construction or personal feeling, so the schools disagree.

en.title: Destination Competitiveness and Governance
en.short: Models of competitiveness, governance networks, branding and how to judge destination rankings.

sections.heading: Competitiveness models
sections.text:
Destination competitiveness is the ability to attract visitors, earn income and use resources well over time. Porter’s diamond explains advantage through factor conditions, demand, related industries and firm rivalry. Ritchie and Crouch (2003) place core resources, supporting factors, destination management and policy inside wider competitive and global environments. Dwyer and Kim (2003) separate endowed resources, created resources, supporting factors, management, demand and situational conditions, then link them to market and economic performance.

The models agree that resources alone do not explain success; management and context matter.

sections.heading: Governance and branding
sections.text:
Destination governance is how decisions are coordinated among government, destination marketing organisations (DMOs), firms, communities and NGOs. A governance network can build trust and share information but can blur accountability. A public-private partnership (PPP) is a formal arrangement where public and private parties share investment, risk and responsibility.

Branding builds a consistent identity and promise; image is what visitors perceive. Positioning chooses a distinct place in the target visitor’s mind; a perceptual map plots how visitors see destinations on chosen attributes. A made-up example: a coastal county’s tourism board, hotel association, parks authority and fisherfolk groups agree waste collection and visitor fees. The brand promises clean beaches, so the partnership must deliver them.

sections.heading: Evaluating policy
sections.text:
Policy evaluation asks whether a strategy met its goals, using indicators such as visitor spend, seasonality, local employment and environmental pressure. Composite indices and rankings, such as the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index, summarise many pillars into one score. They help benchmarking but weights are chosen by analysts, data quality varies and small score shifts can change ranks.

Made-up scores out of 100. Destination A: infrastructure 95, sustainability 50. Destination B: infrastructure 60, sustainability 80. Equal weights: A = (95+50)÷2 = 72.5; B = (60+80)÷2 = 70. A ranks first. With 30% infrastructure and 70% sustainability: A = 0.3×95 + 0.7×50 = 63.5; B = 0.3×60 + 0.7×80 = 74. B ranks first. The weights reversed the ranking, so treat indices as questions, not verdicts.

keyPoints: Destination competitiveness models link resources, management and context; resources alone do not explain success.
Porter’s diamond, Ritchie and Crouch, and Dwyer and Kim offer complementary views of competitiveness.
Governance networks coordinate many actors but need clear accountability.
A public-private partnership shares investment, risk and responsibility between public and private parties.
Brand identity is what the destination promises; image is what visitors perceive.
Composite index score = Σ (weight × pillar score); changing weights can reverse ranks.

en.title: Tourism Analytics and Forecasting
en.short: Forecasting demand with time series and regression, seasonality, big data and tourism satellite accounts.

sections.heading: Forecasting demand
sections.text:
Demand forecasting estimates future visitor numbers, nights or spending for planning capacity and staffing. A time series is a set of observations at equal intervals, split into trend, seasonal, cyclical and irregular parts. Simple methods are the naive forecast (next period equals this one), moving averages and exponential smoothing, which weights recent values more.

Regression relates demand to explanatory variables such as income, prices, exchange rates and past arrivals. Demand is often modelled with both sides in logarithms (log-log), so coefficients read as elasticities. Always report error, such as mean absolute percentage error (MAPE).

sections.heading: Seasonality and a worked example
sections.text:
Seasonality is a repeating pattern within the year. A seasonal index compares a period’s average with the overall average: index = period average ÷ overall average.

Quarterly arrivals at a made-up resort average 240, 480, 560 and 320, so the overall average is 400. The indices are 0.60, 1.20, 1.40 and 0.80, summing to 4.00. If next year’s total is forecast at 2,000, the quarterly average is 500, giving 500 × 0.60 = 300, 600, 700 and 400. Check: 300 + 600 + 700 + 400 = 2,000.

sections.heading: Big data and social media
sections.text: Big data means datasets too large for ordinary tools, described by volume, velocity and variety. Tourism sources include mobile phone location records, card transactions, online search and booking data, and social media posts and reviews. Sentiment analysis classifies review text as positive or negative. Such sources are cheap and timely but rarely random samples, so they carry coverage bias; privacy law and platform access limit them.

sections.heading: Satellite accounts and statistics
sections.text: A tourism satellite account (TSA) is a statistical framework, standardised by the UN and UN Tourism, that measures tourism’s contribution within a country’s national accounts. It links tourism consumption to tourism-characteristic products such as accommodation and air transport, and reports tourism direct gross value added. It measures only the direct contribution, so it is not directly comparable with the World Travel and Tourism Council’s modelled estimates, which include indirect and induced effects. Implementation and coverage differ by country: check the national statistics office.

keyPoints: Seasonal index = period average ÷ overall average; indices for a full year sum to the number of periods.
Forecast for a period = forecast period average × seasonal index.
In a log-log regression, coefficients are elasticities of demand.
MAPE = average of |actual − forecast| ÷ actual, expressed as a percentage.
Big data sources are rarely random samples, so they carry coverage bias.
A TSA measures tourism’s direct contribution inside national accounts; it is not the same as modelled WTTC estimates.

en.title: Research Methods for the Dissertation
en.short: Literature review, conceptual framework, mixed methods, rigour, ethics, data management, writing and defence.

sections.heading: Review to framework
sections.text: A master’s literature review is not a list of summaries. It searches systematically, records the search terms and databases, and synthesises findings by theme. The aim is to show what is known, where authors disagree and which gap your question addresses. From that synthesis you build a conceptual framework: a diagram or narrative that defines the key constructs and proposes how they relate. It guides design and analysis and must be consistent with the literature, not invented after the data.

sections.heading: Mixed methods and rigour
sections.text:
Mixed methods combine quantitative and qualitative strands in one design. They may be sequential, where one strand informs the next, or convergent, where both run in parallel and are then integrated. Integration means comparing and explaining, not reporting two separate studies. In quantitative work, validity asks whether an instrument measures the intended construct; reliability asks whether it gives consistent results. Qualitative work is judged by trustworthiness: credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability. Triangulation, using more than one source or method, strengthens both.

Case: Amina studies guest satisfaction in Kano hotels. She surveys guests and interviews managers. Her framework links service quality to satisfaction through staff responsiveness. She analyses each strand, then uses interviews to explain the survey pattern.

sections.heading: Ethics and data
sections.text: Ethics approval must come before data collection. An ethics committee checks informed consent, confidentiality, risk to participants and the handling of vulnerable groups. Data management covers the whole life of the data. Write a data management plan: what you collect, how you anonymise it, where you store it, who can access it and when you delete it. Data protection law differs by country, so follow your institution’s policy and the national law that applies. Keep backups and clear file names.

sections.heading: Writing and defence
sections.text: A dissertation is an argument, not a diary. Each chapter should have a purpose. Write methods so another researcher could repeat the study. In the defence, examiners test your choices, limitations and contribution. Prepare answers on design, rigour and what you would change.

keyPoints: A literature review synthesises themes and identifies a gap; it is not a list of summaries.
A conceptual framework defines constructs and proposes their relationships, and it must follow from the literature.
Mixed methods integrate quantitative and qualitative strands rather than reporting them separately.
Quantitative work uses validity and reliability; qualitative work uses trustworthiness criteria.
Ethics approval and a data management plan are needed before data collection, and data protection rules vary by country.
The defence tests your understanding of design choices, limitations and contribution.
